**Example material · Synthetic observations · 18 October 2026**

## When the denominator moves

Precision is a property of a calculation. Relevance is a property of the question. Confusing them produces an impressive looking answer to something nobody needed to know.

In this invented example, North has more completed orders than South. Once we divide by eligible opportunities, South has the higher completion rate. Neither figure is wrong; they answer different questions. A useful report keeps the numerator and denominator close enough for the reader to inspect both.

```chart
type: bar
title: "Completion rate (%)"
data:
  inline:
    - {category: "North", value: 78}
    - {category: "South", value: 84}
    - {category: "East", value: 72}
    - {category: "West", value: 81}
encoding: {x: category, y: value}
axes:
  x: {label: Category}
  y: {label: "Completion rate (%)"}
```

*Source: The percentages are fictional. Each represents 100 eligible opportunities, so the chart can be read directly as completions per hundred.*

A real export would come from a file such as `https://data.example.org/exports/completion/2026/10/eligible_opportunities_by_region_and_channel.csv`, with one row per region and channel:

| Region | Channel | Eligible opportunities | Completed orders | Completion rate | Definition version | Last reviewed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| North | Partner storefront | 100 | 78 | 78% | eligibility-rule-2026-10 | 2026-10-18 |
| South | Direct marketplace | 100 | 84 | 84% | eligibility-rule-2026-10 | 2026-10-18 |

## What to take away

Before comparing teams, check that eligibility is defined in the same way. If the rule changes, publish the change with the data. A stable visual identity should never conceal a moving definition.
